segments.text: Right, I'll let you go in a moment, but first, a quick request. This afternoon you'll get an email with a link to our mid-semester feedback survey. It takes about five minutes, and it's anonymous, so I won't know who wrote what. Now, this isn't the official evaluation you fill in at the end of term. This one comes straight to me, and I use it to adjust the course while you're still taking it. Last year, for instance, students asked for more worked examples, so I added them. The survey closes on Sunday night, and on Monday I'll tell you what I plan to change.

Plants have a problem that animals don't. When something comes along to eat them, they can't run away. So, how does a plant protect itself? Well, the first line of defense is physical. Think of the thorns on a rose, or the tough, waxy surface of a holly leaf. Some leaves are even covered in tiny hairs that make it hard for small insects to walk on them. The second line is chemical. Many plants fill their leaves with substances that taste bitter or are actually poisonous. Caffeine is a good example. We enjoy it in coffee and tea, but the plant makes it to poison insects that chew on its leaves. Now, here's the part I find most impressive. Some plants call for help. When caterpillars start chewing on a corn plant, the damaged leaves release a scent into the air. That scent attracts a certain kind of wasp, and the wasps attack the caterpillars. In other words, the plant is sending out a signal that says, 'Your lunch is over here.' And all of this costs the plant energy, which is why many plants don't produce these chemicals all the time. They wait until they're actually attacked. So next time you walk past a quiet green field, remember, it's not as peaceful as it looks.

Here's a price tag that every one of you has seen a thousand times. A shirt costs nineteen ninety-nine. Not twenty dollars. Why? It's only one cent. Well, marketers have a name for this: charm pricing. And there are two main reasons it works. The first is the way we read numbers. We read from left to right, and our brain starts judging the price as soon as it sees the first digit. So nineteen ninety-nine gets filed under 'nineteen-something,' not 'twenty.' Researchers call this the left-digit effect. And notice, it only works when the first digit changes. Dropping a price from three sixty to three fifty-nine does almost nothing. The second reason is what a nine signals. Over the years, shoppers have learned to connect prices ending in nine with sales and discounts. In one well-known experiment, a clothing catalog offered the same dress at thirty-four, thirty-nine, and forty-four dollars. Which sold best? The thirty-nine-dollar one. It even beat the cheaper price. Now, does that mean every store should use nines? Not quite. Have a look at the menu in an expensive restaurant, or the price tag on a luxury watch. You'll usually see round numbers there. A round price says quality, and a nine says discount. So the right ending depends on what you want your customers to think.

Attention, all master's and doctoral students who plan to graduate this spring. The Graduate School's final deadline for submitting a thesis is April twenty-fourth, and I should stress that no extensions will be granted. Before you can submit, however, your document must pass a format check, which covers margins, page numbering, and the reference list. That check takes up to five working days, and in our experience roughly half of all theses are sent back for corrections at least once. So, realistically, if you haven't uploaded your draft for checking by the tenth, you're cutting it very fine. The format guidelines are on the Graduate School website.

So here's the obvious problem. A black hole, by definition, gives off no light. Its gravity is so strong that nothing that falls in can get back out, not even light itself. So how on earth do you find something you can't see? The short answer is, you watch what it does to its surroundings. One approach is to track stars. At the center of our galaxy, astronomers spent years following a handful of stars that whip around an empty-looking point at tremendous speeds. From those orbits, they worked out that the invisible object must have the mass of about four million suns, packed into a tiny region. Nothing else we know of fits that description. A second clue is X-rays. When a black hole pulls gas off a neighboring star, that gas doesn't drop straight in. It spirals, and as it does, it heats up to millions of degrees and glows in X-rays. And then there's a much more recent method, which, frankly, still gives me goosebumps. In twenty fifteen, detectors picked up gravitational waves, tiny ripples in space itself, produced when two black holes collided more than a billion years ago. So notice the pattern here. In none of these cases are we observing the black hole directly. We're inferring it, the way you'd infer wind from the movement of the trees.

segments.text: I want to start today with a ship. According to the ancient writer Plutarch, the people of Athens kept the ship of their hero Theseus for centuries as a kind of monument. Wood rots, of course, so whenever a plank decayed, they swapped in a new one. Now suppose that, in the end, not a single original plank is left. Is it still the ship of Theseus? Hands up if you say yes. Hmm, most of you. OK. Now let me spoil your confidence. In the seventeenth century, Thomas Hobbes added a twist. Suppose somebody had quietly collected every old plank as it was removed, and then put them all back together. Now there are two ships. Which one is the real one? If you think a thing is just its material, you have to pick the rebuilt pile of old wood. If you think what matters is a continuous history, an unbroken story, you'll stay with the ship that was repaired. And notice, this isn't really about boats. Many of the cells in your body have been replaced since you were a child, and yet you'd insist you're the same person. I'm not going to hand you a solution, by the way. Philosophers have been arguing over this one for two thousand years, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who tells you it's settled.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: You have agreed to take part in a research study about volunteering and community. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

Thanks for making time for this interview. First, I'd like to hear about your own experience. Please tell me about a time when you helped someone in your community or took part in a volunteer activity. What did you do, and how did you feel afterward?
Some people like to volunteer as part of a large, organized group, while others prefer to help in small, informal ways, such as assisting a neighbor. Which do you prefer, and why?

Let's turn to your opinion now. It is sometimes said that volunteering mainly benefits the volunteer, for example because it looks good on a job application, rather than the community. Do you agree? Why or why not?

Here is my last question. In many towns, volunteers do jobs such as cleaning parks or running the local library. Should work like this be left to volunteers, or should local governments pay people to do it? Why?
